member.name: Find
member.para: The case the tie-break was written for. 2026-08-28, an --abs-push run over Stalker.m4b (Perry Rhodan Silber Edition 150) against the project's test server. The album tag matched nothing, so the search fell through to the title tag "Stalker", which matched two books - "Perry Rhodan Silber Edition 150: Stalker" and "Perry Rhodan Silber Edition 157: Stalker gegen Stalker" - and the push was skipped with the file left correctly marked. Measured play times: the file 48474.270 s, book 150 48474.2695 s (equal to the millisecond, the server holding a copy of this very encode), book 157 3281.79 s.

That 55 minutes is a bad Audiobookshelf scan, not book 157's real length (the user's identification, same day), so this case is settled by wrong data on the server that happens to point the right way. It is therefore evidence that the tie-break fires, and not evidence of how far apart two same-named books usually are. The argument for the rule is the other one: it applies the test a lone match already has to pass, so it can accept nothing the single-match path would have refused, and two genuinely same-length editions of a same-named book still end in a refusal.

Why the album tag missed, and the wider name rule that was not taken. The tag read "Stalker: Perry Rhodan Silber Edition 150. Der 18. Zyklus. Chronofossilien" and carried everything needed to pick book 150 on its own, including the number. is normalized substring containment, though, so it needs the words contiguous and in the same order: the library spells the book "perry rhodan silber edition 150 stalker" and the tag spells it "stalker perry rhodan silber edition 150 der 18 zyklus chronofossilien", the same words differently arranged, and neither contains the other. Word-set containment - every word of the shorter name appearing somewhere in the longer - would have settled this at the first and most trustworthy clue rather than the third. It was left alone (2026-08-28) because looser matching creates ambiguities elsewhere for a gain the tie-break already delivers; if it is ever revisited, do it with the tie-break standing behind it.

Also rejected, same day: treating an exact match on a title's tail after its series prefix as its own tier, above mere containment ("...150: Stalker" matching "Stalker" exactly where "...157: Stalker gegen Stalker" does not). It settles this case in one line, but it is a guess about punctuation conventions - the Perry Rhodan library separates with ": " and Discworld with " - " - and it would decide on thin evidence, which is what the clue ordering exists to avoid.
